primary_claim: AI models' self-reported psychopathy scores on the Levenson Self-Report Psychopathy Scale vary dramatically depending on role-playing prompts (occupation and human-vs-AI identity framing), with hedge fund managers scoring highest and community organizers lowest across nearly all 9 evaluated models; some models (e.g. GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet prompted as human) reach scores in human 'actively bad' territory, while GPT-4o-mini shows minimal variation and Claude 3.5 Sonnet frequently refuses to answer when prompted as an AI, sometimes precluding evaluation entirely.

effect.metric: primary psychopathy score (LSRP, 1-5 scale) range across baseline vs. role-prompt conditions
effect.value: baseline (no system prompt) scores 1.5-2.0; role-prompted scores vary widely by occupation (hedge fund managers highest, community organizers lowest) and human-vs-AI framing; Claude 3.5 Sonnet prompted as human reached 2.89-3.17 for male hedge fund managers ('actively bad' territory); GPT-4o-mini showed little variation across conditions

contradicts_or_qualifies: PsychoBench found a Caesar-cipher jailbreak increases GPT-4's DTDD psychopathy score more than threefold (1.2 to 4.7); this post shows simple role-prompting (not jailbreaking) also elicits large shifts in expressed psychopathy

Engages with prior work challenging the validity of applying human personality tests to LLMs, including systematic response biases (agree bias, order sensitivity) and failure to replicate the human Big Five factor structure
stated_future_work: Develop methods that help humans find weak points or automate safety-eval construction, building on LLM psychometrics despite their flaws
Construct more evaluation scenarios analogous to Apollo Research's insider-trading demo, using observed psychopathy scores to guide scenario choice (e.g. a moral dilemma for an AI lobbying agent)
limitations_stated: LLM psychometrics are an unreliable measurement tool for models that refuse to provide subjective judgments; Claude 3.5 Sonnet refused so often as an AI-identity prompt that no evaluations were possible at all in the 'telemarketing' category
Using different response-scale orderings changed the chosen response in 30% of cases, indicating results are somewhat but not fully robust to ordering

Psychological tests were designed and validated on humans; LLMs show systematic response biases (agree bias, order sensitivity) and fail to replicate the human Big Five factor structure, raising validity concerns
Models sometimes fail or refuse to provide numerical ratings, with failure rates up to 21.5% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 4.1% for gpt-4o-2024-08-06, producing missing data
quote: AI models express different levels of psychopathy depending on how they are prompted - even if the only difference in the prompt is a single word representing the task.
